subject: Economics
description: Income tax, corporate tax, capital gains, TDS, DTAA, new vs old regime

questions.stem: A direct tax is a tax that:

options.option_text: Is levied on goods and services consumed
Falls directly on the income or wealth of an individual / entity, with the burden NOT shifted to anyone else
Is collected by states only
Is paid only by salaried employees

questions.explanation: Direct tax — burden cannot be shifted; the legal taxpayer is the actual bearer. Examples: Income Tax, Corporate Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Securities Transaction Tax (STT), gift tax (now part of income tax). Indirect tax — burden shifted to consumer; examples: GST, customs duty, excise (now mostly subsumed in GST). India's tax buoyancy has improved post-2017 (GST rollout). Direct-tax-to-GDP ratio target: 6%+; FY 2023-24 actual ~6.6% — record level. Administered by CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes) under Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The administration of direct taxes in India is the responsibility of:

options.option_text: CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs)
CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes)
RBI (Reserve Bank of India)
SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)

questions.explanation: CBDT — statutory body under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963; under Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. Administers Income Tax Act 1961 + related laws. Headed by Chairperson + 6 members (IRS officers). CBIC — handles GST + Customs (since GST replaced the old Central Excise role). RBI — monetary policy + banking regulation. SEBI — securities market regulator. CBDT and CBIC together form the 'Two Boards' under the Department of Revenue.

questions.stem: Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) on listed equity shares (held > 12 months) is taxed at the rate of (post-Budget 2024-25):

options.option_text: 10% above ₹1 lakh
12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh exemption (revised in July 2024 budget)
20% above ₹2 lakh
Exempt entirely

questions.explanation: Budget 2024 (July 2024, post-elections) revised LTCG and STCG rates. LTCG on listed equity / equity MFs (>12 months): now 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh exemption (was 10% above ₹1 lakh). STCG on listed equity (≤12 months): now 20% (was 15%). LTCG on other assets (real estate, gold, debt MFs etc.): 12.5% (was 20% with indexation; indexation removed for transfers after 23-Jul-2024 except some real-estate grandfathering). Holding period harmonised: listed securities 12 months, all others 24 months.

questions.stem: TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) on bank interest above the threshold is governed by which section?

options.option_text: Section 80C
Section 194A
Section 234B
Section 10(14)

questions.explanation: Section 194A — TDS on interest other than securities (bank deposits, etc.). Threshold raised in Budget 2025 — to ₹50,000/year (general; was ₹40,000) and ₹1,00,000/year for senior citizens (was ₹50,000). Common 194-series sections: 194 (dividends), 194A (interest), 194C (contractor), 194H (commission), 194J (professional fees), 194Q (purchase of goods >₹50 lakh), 194R (perquisites), 194S (virtual digital assets — crypto). Section 80C — deduction (not TDS); 234B — interest on default in advance tax; 10(14) — exemption on specified allowances.

questions.stem: The base corporate tax rate for domestic companies (NOT opting for 22% concessional regime, turnover > ₹400 cr) plus surcharge and cess is approximately:

options.option_text: 15% (the new manufacturing rate)
30% base, with 22% concessional rate available under Section 115BAA (no exemptions)
40% (foreign companies only)

questions.explanation: Domestic companies (turnover > ₹400 cr previous year): 30% base + cess + surcharge ≈ 34.94% effective. Companies opting for 115BAA (introduced Sep 2019): 22% + 10% surcharge + 4% cess = 25.17% effective, but they must forgo most exemptions and deductions. New manufacturing companies (incorporated after 1-Oct-2019, started mfg by 31-Mar-2024) under 115BAB: 15%+10%+4% = 17.16%. Smaller domestic companies (turnover ≤ ₹400 cr in PY 2022-23): 25% base. Foreign companies: 35% base (post Budget 2024, reduced from 40%) + surcharge + cess.

questions.stem: DTAA (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement) is a bilateral treaty that:

options.option_text: Doubles the tax rate for dual-resident individuals
Prevents the same income from being taxed twice (in source country and residence country) and helps allocate taxing rights
Allows tax evasion legally
Imposes uniform tax rates worldwide

questions.explanation: DTAA — bilateral; India has DTAAs with 90+ countries. Methods: (1) Exemption — income taxed only in one country; (2) Credit — both tax, but resident country gives credit for foreign tax paid. Mauritius DTAA was historically misused for round-tripping; renegotiated via Protocol 2016 (capital gains taxable in source country from 1-Apr-2017). India follows the OECD-modelled UN Model. GAAR (General Anti-Avoidance Rules) — overrides treaty if tax-avoidance is the main purpose. Section 90 of the Income Tax Act empowers the Government to enter into DTAAs.

questions.stem: The 'New Tax Regime' (Section 115BAC), made the default regime from FY 2023-24, is characterised by:

options.option_text: Higher slab rates and most deductions allowed
Lower slab rates BUT most deductions/exemptions (80C, HRA, LTA, etc.) NOT allowed; standard deduction allowed
Same as old regime
Applicable only to corporates

questions.explanation: New Tax Regime — Section 115BAC, introduced Budget 2020, made default from FY 2023-24 (AY 2024-25). Lower slab rates but nearly all major deductions (80C, 80D, HRA, LTA, home-loan interest under 24(b), etc.) NOT allowed — only standard deduction (₹75,000 for FY 2024-25), employer NPS contribution (80CCD(2)), and family-pension deduction. FY 2025-26 slabs (post Feb 2025 budget): 0-₹4L nil; ₹4-8L 5%; ₹8-12L 10%; ₹12-16L 15%; ₹16-20L 20%; ₹20-24L 25%; >₹24L 30%. Rebate under 87A — full rebate up to ₹12L taxable income (so effectively no tax up to ₹12.75L with std deduction). Old regime still optionally available.

questions.stem: Under the Old Tax Regime, what is the basic income tax exemption limit for a resident senior citizen aged 60 years or more but less than 80 years?

options.option_text: ₹2,50,000 — equal to the limit for general category taxpayers
₹3,00,000 — enhanced limit for citizens aged 60 to 79 years
₹5,00,000 — limit reserved for super-senior citizens aged 80+
₹3,50,000 — a midpoint between general and super-senior limits

questions.explanation: Under the Old Tax Regime, the basic exemption limit is ₹3,00,000 for senior citizens (60–79 years), compared to ₹2,50,000 for general taxpayers. The ₹5,00,000 limit (Option C) applies only to super-senior citizens aged 80 and above. Option D (₹3,50,000) does not correspond to any prescribed bracket and is a plausible-sounding trap for candidates who guess a midpoint.

questions.stem: An individual taxpayer is liable to pay advance tax in a financial year only if the estimated tax payable (after TDS) exceeds which threshold?

options.option_text: ₹5,000 — a threshold more relevant to TDS compliance rules
₹10,000 — the statutory trigger for advance tax installments
₹25,000 — the prescribed ceiling for self-assessment tax only
₹50,000 — a limit said to apply only to business taxpayers

questions.explanation: Section 208 of the Income Tax Act mandates payment of advance tax when estimated tax liability for the year exceeds ₹10,000 after deducting TDS. ₹5,000 (Option A) has no statutory relevance here. ₹25,000 and ₹50,000 are common distractors but have no basis in advance tax provisions. Note: resident senior citizens (75+) with only pension/interest income are exempt from advance tax under Section 207.

questions.stem: Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) under Section 115JB was reduced by the Finance Act, 2019. What is the current rate of MAT applicable to domestic companies?

options.option_text: 10% of book profit, aimed at curbing large-scale tax avoidance
15% of book profit, plus applicable surcharge and cess
18.5% of book profit, the rate that applied before FY 2019-20
20% of book profit, aligned with the concessional corporate rate

questions.explanation: The Finance Act, 2019 reduced MAT from 18.5% to 15% of book profit (plus surcharge and health/education cess). Option C (18.5%) is the pre-2019 rate and is the most tempting distractor since many textbooks still cite it. MAT applies when a company's normal income-tax liability falls below 15% of its book profit, ensuring a minimum tax floor. Companies opting for the Section 115BAA/115BAB concessional regimes are exempt from MAT.

questions.stem: The additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 available for contributions to the National Pension System (NPS) under Section 80CCD(1B) is best described as:

options.option_text: Subsumed within the overall ₹1.5 lakh ceiling under Section 80C
Available over and above the ₹1.5 lakh limit of Section 80C/80CCD(1)
Restricted exclusively to central and state government employees
Claimable only for employer NPS contributions routed via Section 80CCD(2)

questions.explanation: Section 80CCD(1B) provides an exclusive additional deduction of ₹50,000 for voluntary NPS contributions by any individual (not just government employees), which is over and above the ₹1.5 lakh ceiling of Section 80C/80CCD(1). This makes the effective NPS-linked deduction potentially ₹2,00,000. Option A is the most common mistake — candidates conflate 80CCD(1B) with the 80C basket. Option C is wrong because private-sector employees can also claim it. Option D describes 80CCD(2), a separate employer-contribution deduction.

questions.stem: Winnings from lotteries, card games, and crossword puzzles are taxed under Section 115BB of the Income Tax Act. Which statement correctly describes the tax treatment?

options.option_text: Taxed at 20% flat; a standard deduction of ₹50,000 is permitted
Taxed at 25% flat; prior gambling losses can be set off against wins
Taxed at 30% flat; no deduction or basic exemption benefit applies
Taxed at 35% flat only when aggregate winnings exceed ₹10 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 115BB imposes a flat 30% tax on gross winnings from lotteries, puzzles, card games, and similar activities. Crucially, no deductions (including Chapter VI-A) are allowed, and the basic exemption limit does not apply — even a first-rupee win triggers taxation. Option B is wrong because gambling losses cannot be set off or carried forward under Indian income tax law. Options A and D involve incorrect rates and thresholds that do not exist in the Act.

questions.stem: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR), effective from Assessment Year 2018-19, grant the Income Tax Department the authority to:

options.option_text: Deny DTAA benefits only after tax evasion is proved in a court of law
Disregard any arrangement where obtaining a tax benefit is the main purpose
Levy a 40% penalty automatically on undisclosed income during tax raids
Subject foreign companies in tax havens to domestic Minimum Alternate Tax

questions.explanation: GAAR (Sections 95–102, Income Tax Act) empowers authorities to disregard, recharacterise, or restructure any 'impermissible avoidance arrangement' — one whose main purpose or one of its main purposes is to obtain a tax benefit. Crucially, GAAR can override DTAA provisions without requiring court proof (contra Option A), shifting the burden of proof to the taxpayer to demonstrate commercial substance. Option C describes search and seizure penalties (Section 271AAB), a different provision entirely. Option D conflates MAT applicability with GAAR.

questions.stem: Section 92C of the Income Tax Act prescribes specific methods for computing the arm's length price in international transactions between associated enterprises. Which of the following is NOT among the prescribed methods?

options.option_text: Resale Price Method (RPM) for distribution-chain transactions
Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) for routine service deals
Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP) based on third-party comparables
Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) method for valuing intangible asset transfers

questions.explanation: The six prescribed Transfer Pricing methods under Section 92C are: CUP, Resale Price Method (RPM), Cost Plus Method (CPM), Profit Split Method (PSM), Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM), and 'any other method' (Rule 10AB). Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) is a valuation technique used in finance and business contexts but is not one of the six enumerated methods under Section 92C. Candidates familiar with corporate finance often incorrectly identify DCF as a prescribed TP method, making it an effective hard distractor.
